tweets.text:
My essay on why we invested in Pangram at Menlo: https://t.co/BqJAPFDRos
Pangram 4 Launch: https://t.co/JqWGFDKiQf
Pangram Image Preview: https://t.co/MsT7fIN70G
New York Times announcement: https://t.co/sUtCkcvwbw
TechCrunch announcement: https://t.co/qzzL8n23i7

AI-generated content is 35-50% of the internet. As the cost of producing language falls to zero, the cost of *trusting* language goes to infinity.

I’m genuinely so excited to announce that we’re leading a round in Pangram to fix this, and launching two big new models!
– Pangram 4, a 6x bigger AI detection model that beats “humanized” text and boasts a 1 in 10,000 false positive rate and even scales to the newest model releases like Opus 5, Fable and GPT 5.6 Sol. Try asking an LLM to write like a human on loop, and it still won’t break it.

– Pangram Image Preview, the best attempt we've seen at detecting AI images. Images can be tricky because you can add small AI changes to real photos, but this tackles even that. r/isthisAI is a top 25 AI subreddit dedicated to humans asking this question.

Today, Substack, Quora, Google Classroom, Internet Archive and even NeurIPS rely on Pangram for their AI detection. The myth that all detection systems are unreliable because they misclassify historical docs is promulgated by inferior services that do not take Pangram's bitter lesson-pilled deep learning approach to the problem.

The business has grown 35x in the last year and >5x since even the last funding round. The founders Max Spero and Bradley Emi met at Stanford and went on do mission critical work at Nuro and be on the early Tesla Autopilot team with Andrej Karpathy. I love that they could’ve raised any amount of money (we all see the monster funding rounds) but despite being way farther ahead, chose to build the company gradually and sustainably, proving that it can still be done.

Whether you like AI or not, we can all agree the user has the right to know and decide for themselves and choose whether they want to read it. This has applications through social networks, research publications, book publishers, pedagogy and even for cleaning data in labs. It's a deeply important problem to humanity. This is why Pangram is so close to my heart.
